summary: Defines protocol and deployment requirements for the DNS root name service, a critical part of Internet architecture. Operational requirements are out of scope.

eli5.summary: The very top of the Internet's phone book needs rules, and this says what they are.

questions: what are the dns root service requirements
what does the dns root name service need to do
what is the dns root name service
what are the dns root server requirements
subtitle: The short list of protocol and deployment rules every DNS root name service must follow.

tldr.problem: RFC 2870 mixed protocol and operational requirements for root name servers, and both had evolved since it was published.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 7720 keeps only the protocol requirements and a few deployment requirements, as MUST rules. Operational requirements moved to RSSAC-001.
tldr.outcome: It obsoletes RFC 2870. Together with RSSAC-001 it functionally replaces that document.

today: RFC 7720 is a Best Current Practice (BCP 40) published in December 2015, and it obsoletes RFC 2870. The unit metadata shows no later RFC obsoleting or updating it.

sections.title: Why the Root Needs Requirements
sections.content:
The DNS root name service is described as a critical part of the Internet architecture. The root servers are authoritative servers of the unique root zone ("."). The RFC notes they currently also serve the root-servers.net zone, and some also serve the zone for the .arpa top-level domain.

This document describes the external interface of the root name servers from a protocol viewpoint. It sets basic requirements for what DNS clients can expect when they talk to a root name service over the public Internet. It uses the RFC 2119 keywords such as MUST and SHOULD.
sections.eli5: The root servers are the first place the Internet's phone book looks things up. This note says what they have to be good at.

sections.title: Relationship to RFC 2870
sections.content:
RFC 2870 covered both protocol and operational requirements for root name servers. Since it was published, both sets of requirements evolved, so the authors found it made more sense to split them into two documents.

This document defines only the protocol requirements and some deployment requirements. The operational requirements from RFC 2870 were removed. They are now defined by the Root Server System Advisory Committee (RSSAC) of ICANN in RSSAC-001. This document obsoletes RFC 2870, and the two documents together functionally replace it.
sections.eli5: One old rulebook tried to cover everything. Now it is split in two: this one has the technical rules, and another group writes the day-to-day running rules.

sections.title: Protocol Requirements
sections.content:
These are the minimum high-level protocol requirements. Operative details are in RSSAC-001. The root name service MUST:

  • implement core DNS (RFC 1035) and the clarifications to the DNS (RFC 2181);
  • support IPv4 and IPv6 transport of DNS queries and responses;
  • support UDP and TCP transport of DNS queries and responses;
  • generate checksums when sending UDP datagrams, and verify checksums when receiving UDP datagrams that contain a non-zero checksum;
  • implement DNSSEC as an authoritative name service;
  • implement the extension mechanisms for DNS, EDNS(0).
sections.eli5: The root servers must speak the basic DNS language, work over both old and new Internet addresses, and be able to prove their answers are genuine.

sections.title: Deployment Requirements
sections.content:
Two deployment rules apply. The root name service MUST answer queries from any entity conforming to RFC 1122 with a valid IP address. It also MUST serve the unique root zone.

In practice this means the service may not pick and choose which conforming hosts it answers, and it may not serve some alternative root zone in place of the single one.
sections.eli5: The root servers have to answer anyone who asks properly, and they all have to hand out the same one official list.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The document does not specify a new protocol. It points out that the root name service is a key component of the Internet architecture and plays a key role in the overall security of the Internet.

Security considerations for the DNS protocols are in their own specifications. Security considerations on the operational side of the root name servers are discussed in RSSAC-001.
sections.eli5: The top of the phone book matters for everyone's safety, so the detailed safety rules live in the documents about each part.

items.title: UDP checksums
items.text: Generate on send; verify when non-zero on receipt.

items.title: DNSSEC
items.text: Implemented as an authoritative name service.
